doc.title: Bob Haggart interviewed by Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, September 22, 1995

title: Jam sessions and early heroes
summary: Early school jamming, his first eight-dollar bass job, and idols Bud Freeman, Goodman, Teagarden and Hawkins.

bands.name: Red Nichols and His Five Pennies

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: I wanted to ask you something that I’d like to relate to our students. You know, many times people didn’t understand how necessary jam sessions were but that’s where you could work out your ideas. Tell us about jam sessions.

We used to do quite a lot of that, get together and play. I know that when I was just learning the bass we’d go into the auditorium when nothing was happening, go down to the bottom of the auditorium there and this trombone player and I would play tunes. He was just learning “Jazz Me Blues” and tunes like that, and I was just learning the bass, I had just learned the scale. So I was learning to play in B flat. He showed me the C scale. And then I went from there, the first Saturday night I got a job on the bass, right away, made eight bucks. I don’t know what I was doing, but it was fun, and so that started me off. But you have to get together. When I hear kids say how do you do this, what do you — I say well you find a guy who likes to play and the two of you get together and get a third guy, and you try to play songs, you play tunes. Let’s try to play this, you know, and you all listen to records, and that’s the way it happened with me anyway, it’s — all like the same things. I was crazy about Bud Freeman and I first heard Red Nichols and his Five Pennies with Jimmy Dorsey on the clarinet, and then I heard Benny Goodman for God’s sake, he was unbelievable in those days, way out front in a class by himself. He was just a kid in his 20s. And Jack Teagarden, I couldn’t believe, before that it was Miff Mole, he was around New York and Jack came in to town and turned it all around, Teagarden. Bud Freeman, on the tenor sax, and Coleman Hawkins, he and Coleman Hawkins were the two stars at that time. Later Lester Young you know, Chu Berry, Coltrane. Everything goes in stages, you know.
